catalog_quote: Evidence for lexical stress in Muyu varies. Both Drabbe (1954) and Christensen (2013) report the existence of non-phonemic accent/stress on the lexeme level for their respective dialect. According to Drabbe, an “accent” (which is not further specified) is on the last syllable of each word, and a “minor accent” (i.e. secondary stress) on the first syllable of a trisyllabic word. [...] Probably the Ninati and Metomka dialects (Drabbe) have a different system for lexical stress than Yonggom (Christensen). However, our findings for the Kawip dialect point in another direction. It seems that speakers of Kawip do not assign lexical stress at all. Although we did not investigate the topic systematically, there are two kinds of (very preliminary) evidence for a lack of lexical stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Kawiyet/Kawip dialect Zahrer finds no lexical (word) stress: consultants accept /'yu.lun/ and /yu.'lun/ equally, and pitch/intensity of the word yulun across four speakers show no consistently prominent syllable; Muyu also has no lexical tone (unlike Mountain Ok). Prosody works at the utterance level (boundary tones L% final vs H% non-final/question, sec. 2.4.3). The only word-level accent is morphological: the verb suffixes -d DUR and -n SS attract a pitch accent onto the immediately preceding vowel, yielding near-minimal pairs such as bomá-n-up 'we walked and..' vs bom-an-up 'we will walk' (where the irrealis form keeps its accent on the last syllable, p. 297). Older sources on other dialects differ: Drabbe 1954 (Ninati, Metomka = kts) reports an accent on the last syllable of every word with a minor accent on the first syllable of trisyllables (Healey 1964:61 renders this as primary accent on the final syllable of monomorphemic words and on the final syllable of the first root of compounds, Drabbe 1954:153), and Christensen 2013:4-5 reports Yonggom stress always on the first syllable (trochaic).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None for Kawip (no lexical stress at all). Drabbe (as summarised on p. 51) reported a 'minor accent' on the first syllable of trisyllabic words; Christensen's Yonggom examples carry secondary stresses on alternate syllables (disyllabic trochaic feet).
new_statements.exceptions: Verb suffixes -d 'DUR' and -n 'SS' attract a pitch accent to the preceding vowel (minimal pairs with irrealis -an forms, pp. 53-54, 297); one consultant distinguished éyom 'together with this' from eyóm 'in here' by accent placement (p. 189 fn. 5, flagged by the author as a single-consultant judgement on 'lexical stress which is generally not well understood yet'). Author stresses the evidence is 'very preliminary' and 'a thorough study of Muyu prosody is still outstanding' (p. 51).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexemes uttered in isolation in a reading task, Fig. 2.2; the author notes they were not in a carrier sentence) plus inflected verb forms for the stress-attracting suffixes; intonation described separately at the intonation-unit level. Same conclusion repeated in Zahrer 2025 Children of the sago p. 5: 'there seems to be no lexical stress'.
new_statements.identity_note: The first-hand statement is about the Kawiyet/Kawip dialect of Muyu (villages Upyetetko and Kanggewot, Waropko district, 'centrally in the Muyu area'). Zahrer treats Muyu as one language covering both ISO kti/kts = nort2916/sout2940 and says the kti/kts split rests only on Drabbe's Ninati (north) vs Metomka (south) descriptions; Healey 1964:44 (citing Schoorl) had placed the Kanggewot dialect under Northern Kati (nort2916). So Zahrer's evidence is not specifically Metomka/South Muyu. The sources tied specifically to kts (Drabbe 1954 on Metomka, summarised second-hand by Healey 1964:61 and Zahrer 2025:51; the 1931-32 Holle list 197 for the lower Muyu River, Stokhof 1982:173) report a non-phonemic accent/stress on the LAST syllable, which Zahrer explicitly contrasts with his finding of no lexical stress in Kawip. The same statement should be attached to nort2916 with the same caveat.

sources.note: Sec. 2.4.1 pp. 51-53: Kawip dialect 'does not have lexical stress' (preliminary judgement + pitch/intensity evidence); no lexical tone; summarises Drabbe 1954 (last-syllable accent, minor accent on first syllable of trisyllables) and Christensen 2013 (Yonggom first-syllable stress). Sec. 2.4.2: suffixes -d DUR and -n SS attract a pitch accent on the preceding vowel; boundary tones L%/H% (2.4.3).
